title: Creta. Penates
titleEn: The Plague on Crete and the Dream of the Penates — Aeneid III.99–208
part: The Plague on Crete and the Dream of the Penates (III.99–208)
about: At Delos the Trojans have just heard Apollo's oracle, and joy and confusion break out as they ask which land the god means. Anchises, calling up the old traditions, reads the oracle as pointing to Crete: it lies in the middle of the sea, it holds Mount Ida and the cradle of their race, and it is the island from which their forefather Teucer first came to the Trojan shore, before Ilium stood, along with the worship of the Great Mother, her cymbals, her lions and her faithful silence. He bids them follow the gods' orders, appease the winds and make for Crete; the voyage is short if Jupiter helps. He sacrifices bulls to Neptune and Apollo, a black victim to Storm and a white one to the kindly Zephyrs. A rumour reaches them that Idomeneus has been driven from his father's kingdom and that Crete lies empty, and they sail past Naxos, Donysa, Olearos, Paros and the scattered Cyclades while the sailors shout in rivalry and urge each other on to Crete and their forefathers. Aeneas, landing among the old Curetes, eagerly lays out a city called Pergamum, bids the people love their hearths and build a citadel, and has hardly drawn up the ships and given laws and homes when a wasting plague falls on men, trees and crops, and Sirius scorches the barren fields. Anchises urges a return to the oracle at Delos to ask what end to their toils is intended. That night the sacred images of the Penates, the Trojan household gods he carried from burning Troy, appear to Aeneas as he lies there, plain in the moonlight that pours through the windows, and tell him that Apollo has sent them: they will raise his descendants to the stars and give empire to their city; he must prepare great walls for the great, for Crete was not Apollo's choice. The true home is Hesperia, an ancient land of Oenotrian men, now called Italy, the original seat of Dardanus and Iasius, and Jupiter denies Aeneas the Cretan fields. Stunned, he leaps up, raises his hands to heaven, pours out unspoiled offerings and tells Anchises; the old man sees that he has mistaken the two lines of their ancestry, remembers that only Cassandra ever spoke of Hesperia and Italy, and bids them yield to Phoebus. They leave a few behind and sail, and once the land has vanished, black rain-cloud gathers overhead and a storm scatters the fleet. For three days and nights they wander blind, even Palinurus unable to tell day from night, until on the fourth day land seems to rise and the sailors fall to their oars.

sentences.t: Haec Phoebus;
sentences.l: This Phoebus;
sentences.i: So Phoebus spoke;
sentences.n: The part opens on a new paragraph. 'Haec' is the neuter plural accusative, 'these things', with the verb of speaking understood (the ellipsis of the verb of saying, you'll see this constantly). Aeneas is still telling Dido the story, and the oracle given at Delos in the last part is what 'Phoebus' (Apollo) has just said. The semicolon joins the sentence to the one that follows.

sentences.t:
mixtoque ingens exorta tumultu
laetitia, et cuncti quae sint ea moenia quaerunt,
quo Phoebus vocet errantis iubeatque reverti?
sentences.l:
and mingled with tumult huge arisen
joy, and all ask what those walls may be
to which Phoebus calls the wanderers and bids them turn back?
sentences.i: A great joy rose, mixed with tumult, and all asked what those walls might be to which Phoebus was calling the wanderers and bidding them return.
sentences.n: 'ingens… laetitia' is the subject, with 'exorta' (perfect participle of the deponent 'exorior', 'having risen') split from it by 'mixto… tumultu', an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'mixed with uproar'; the framing of 'ingens' and 'laetitia' round the participle is the effect the literal line keeps. 'Ea' agrees with 'moenia'. 'quae sint' and 'quo… vocet… iubeatque' are indirect questions, so the verbs are subjunctive; the main verb 'quaerunt' is a vivid present, while after 'exorta' the verb 'est' is left out, so 'joy rose' is perfect. 'errantis' is an accusative plural in -is (the wanderers, 'us'), and 'reverti' is the present infinitive of the deponent 'revertor', 'return'. A question mark closes what is really an indirect question; Greenough prints it so.

sentences.t: Tum genitor, veterum volvens monumenta virorum,
sentences.l: Then the father, turning over the records of men of old,
sentences.i: Then Anchises, turning over in his mind the records of men of old,
sentences.n: 'genitor' is 'the father', Anchises, the 'pater' of line 144 is the same man. 'volvens' is the present participle of 'volvo', 'turning over, revolving', as the mind does with memories. 'monumenta' is 'records, memorials', here traditions. 'veterum… virorum' is a genitive plural, 'of the men of old'. 'virorum' is the full genitive plural (the short 'virum' also occurs). The comma holds the sentence open until the speech begins.

sentences.t: “Audite, O proceres ait et spes discite vestras:
sentences.l: “Hear, O chiefs, says he, and learn your hopes:
sentences.i: “Hear me, my lords — so he says — and learn what you may hope:
sentences.n: Anchises' speech begins, with the opening “; it runs to line 117. 'Audite' and 'discite' are imperatives (second plural). 'ait' is the present of the defective verb 'aio', 'he says', thrown into the middle of the speech as a parenthesis; Greenough prints no comma round it. 'proceres' is 'chiefs, leaders', a vocative plural. 'spes… vestras' is 'your hopes', the thing to be learned; the colon announces the explanation that follows.

sentences.t: Creta Iovis magni medio iacet insula ponto;
sentences.l: Crete of great Jupiter in mid sea lies, an island;
sentences.i: In the midst of the sea lies Crete, the island of great Jupiter;
sentences.n: 'Creta' is the subject, and 'insula' stands in apposition to it, set late in the line. 'Iovis magni' is a genitive, 'of great Jupiter', because tradition made the god be born and raised on Crete. 'medio… ponto' is an ablative of place where, 'in the middle of the sea'; 'medio' and 'ponto' frame 'iacet insula', so the island sits in the middle of the words as it does in the sea.

sentences.t: mons Idaeus ubi, et gentis cunabula nostrae.
sentences.l: where is Mount Ida, and the cradle of our race.
sentences.i: where Mount Ida stands, and where our people's cradle lies.
sentences.n: 'ubi' means 'where', and the verb 'est' is understood (a very common ellipsis in Latin). 'mons Idaeus' is the Ida in Crete, not the Trojan one (a second mountain of that name stood in Phrygia, hence the confusion that follows). 'cunabula' is a neuter plural, 'cradle', and 'gentis… nostrae' is a genitive, 'of our race'. The period closes the first sentence of the speech.

sentences.t: Centum urbes habitant magnas, uberrima regna;
sentences.l: A hundred cities they inhabit, great ones, most fertile realms;
sentences.i: A hundred great cities the Cretans hold, realms of the richest soil;
sentences.n: 'habitant' has no stated subject; 'they', the Cretans, is to be understood from 'Creta'. 'Centum urbes' is the object, with 'magnas' placed after it. 'uberrima' is the superlative of 'uber', 'fertile', and 'regna' is in apposition to 'urbes'. The Cretans were said to hold a hundred cities (Homer's 'Crete of a hundred cities').

sentences.t:
maximus unde pater, si rite audita recordor,
Teucrus Rhoeteas primum est advectus in oras,
sentences.l:
from which our greatest father, if rightly the things heard I recall,
Teucrus to the Rhoetean shores first was borne
sentences.i: From it our greatest forefather, if I rightly recall what I have heard, Teucer, first came to the shores of Rhoeteum,
sentences.n: 'unde' is 'from which' (from Crete). 'maximus… pater' is 'our greatest father, ancestor', and 'Teucrus' is the same man as the Teucer of tradition, set after the parenthesis 'si rite audita recordor', 'if I recall rightly the things I have heard'. 'audita' is a neuter plural perfect participle used as a noun. 'Teucrus' is the form of the name that Greenough prints, with the ending -us. 'est advectus' is the perfect passive of 'adveho', 'was carried to'. 'Rhoeteas' is an adjective, 'of Rhoeteum', a headland on the Trojan coast, and so means 'Trojan'.

sentences.t: optavitque locum regno.
sentences.l: and chose a place for his kingdom.
sentences.i: and chose a spot to be his kingdom.
sentences.n: 'optavit' is the perfect of 'opto', 'choose, wish for', joined to the previous clause by '-que'. 'regno' is a dative of purpose, 'for a kingdom'. The sentence ends in mid-line, and the next unit begins on the same line.

sentences.t:
Nondum Ilium et arces
Pergameae steterant;
sentences.l:
Not yet Ilium and the citadels
of Pergamum had stood;
sentences.i: Ilium and its citadels of Pergamum were not yet standing;
sentences.n: 'Nondum' is 'not yet'. 'steterant' is the pluperfect of 'sto', 'had stood'. 'Ilium' is Troy, and 'arces Pergameae' is 'the Pergamean citadels', the citadel of Troy (the plural for a singular is poetic). The point is that Teucer came before Troy was built: Anchises is fitting the Cretan story to the Trojan one.

sentences.t: habitabant vallibus imis.
sentences.l: they were living in the lowest valleys.
sentences.i: the settlers lived in the valleys far below.
sentences.n: 'habitabant' has no stated subject (Teucer and his people). 'vallibus imis' is an ablative of place where, 'in the deepest valleys', that is, before they built on the heights.

sentences.t:
hinc mater cultrix Cybeli Corybantiaque aera
Idaeumque nemus;
sentences.l:
From here the Mother, dweller of Cybelus, and the Corybantian bronzes
and the Idaean grove;
sentences.i: From Crete came the Mother who haunts Cybelus, the bronze cymbals of the Corybantes, and the grove of Ida;
sentences.n: 'hinc' is 'from here', that is, from Crete. The three nominatives are 'mater', 'aera' and 'nemus'; there is no verb, and 'hinc' is repeated in the next clause (anaphora). 'mater cultrix Cybeli' is 'the Mother who dwells on Cybelus' (a Phrygian mountain; 'cultrix' is the feminine of 'cultor', 'dweller, worshipper'). The Great Mother is Cybele; Anchises' claim is that her rites came to Phrygia from Crete. 'Corybantiaque aera' is 'the Corybantian bronzes', the cymbals clashed by her attendants the Corybantes. 'Idaeum nemus' is 'the grove of Ida'. 'aera' is the plural of 'aes', 'bronze'.

sentences.t:
hinc fida silentia sacris,
et iuncti currum dominae subiere leones.
sentences.l:
hence the faithful silence in the rites,
and the yoked lions went under the mistress's chariot.
sentences.i: from there too the faithful silence of the mysteries, and the yoked lions that drew their mistress's chariot.
sentences.n: 'hinc fida silentia sacris' is 'from here the loyal silence for the rites', that is, the secrecy of her mystery. 'sacris' is a dative of reference, 'for the rites'. 'iuncti… leones' is the subject, and 'subiere' is the perfect 'subierunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly), 'went under'. 'currum' is the object: lions came under the chariot's yoke, so that they drew it. 'dominae' is a genitive, 'of their mistress', Cybele.

sentences.t: Ergo agite, et, divom ducunt qua iussa, sequamur;
sentences.l: Therefore come, and, where the gods' commands lead, let us follow;
sentences.i: Come then, and let us follow where the commands of the gods lead;
sentences.n: 'Ergo agite' is 'so come, then' ('agite' is the plural imperative of 'ago'). 'sequamur' is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us follow'. 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'where', and 'divom… iussa' is 'the orders of the gods', the neuter plural subject of 'ducunt'. 'divom' is the old genitive plural for 'divorum' (you'll see this constantly; the Latin Library prints 'diuum', the same word in another spelling).

sentences.t: placemus ventos et Gnosia regna petamus.
sentences.l: let us appease the winds and seek the Gnosian realms.
sentences.i: Let us appease the winds, and seek the realms of Cnossus.
sentences.n: Both verbs are hortatory subjunctives like 'sequamur' ('placemus' from 'placo', 'appease'; 'petamus' from 'peto', 'seek'). 'Gnosia' is the adjective from Cnossus, the capital of Minos, hence 'Cretan'; the Latin Library prints 'Cnosia', the same word. Appeasing the winds is a precaution before sailing.

sentences.t: Nec longo distant cursu;
sentences.l: Nor by a long course do they lie apart;
sentences.i: They lie no long voyage away;
sentences.n: 'Nec' joins to the speech; 'distant' is the plural present of 'disto', 'be apart, distant', with Crete and the Trojans' present position understood as its subject. 'longo… cursu' is an ablative of measure or manner, 'by a long course'.

sentences.t:
modo Iuppiter adsit,
tertia lux classem Cretaeis sistet in oris.”
sentences.l:
only let Jupiter be at hand,
the third day will set the fleet on Cretan shores.”
sentences.i: Only let Jupiter be near, and the third dawn will bring our fleet to rest on Cretan shores.”
sentences.n: 'modo' with the subjunctive 'adsit' (from 'adsum') is a proviso, 'provided only that Jupiter be present'. 'tertia lux' is 'the third day', the third dawn. 'sistet' is the future of 'sisto', 'will set, bring to a stop'. 'Cretaeis… in oris' is 'on Cretan shores'. The closing ” ends Anchises' speech, which opened at 103.

sentences.t: Sic fatus, meritos aris mactavit honores,
sentences.l: So having spoken, he slew on the altars the due honours,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and slew upon the altars the offerings that were due:
sentences.n: 'Sic fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', 'having spoken thus', and is often used to close a speech. 'mactavit' is the perfect of 'macto', 'slaughter as an offering'. 'honores' means 'honours', that is, the victims offered; 'meritos' means 'due, deserved', and 'aris' is a dative (or ablative) of place, 'at the altars'. The list of victims that follows is in apposition to 'honores'.

sentences.t:
taurum Neptuno, taurum tibi, pulcher Apollo
nigram Hiemi pecudem, Zephyris felicibus albam.
sentences.l:
a bull to Neptune, a bull to you, fair Apollo,
a black beast to Storm, a white to the kindly Zephyrs.
sentences.i: a bull for Neptune, a bull for you, beautiful Apollo, a black beast for Storm, a white for the kindly west winds.
sentences.n: All four are datives of the god receiving the offering, with the verb 'mactavit' understood from the last unit. Greenough prints no punctuation after 'Apollo'. 'tibi, pulcher Apollo' is a sudden address to the god in the second person. 'Hiemi' is the dative of 'Hiems', Storm or Winter, a personified weather power. The colours follow Roman practice: black for the gloomy powers, white for the favourable; 'Zephyris felicibus' means 'the kindly west winds'. The black beast is the 'pecudem', a feminine noun; 'albam' agrees with it.

sentences.t:
Fama volat pulsum regnis cessisse paternis
Idomenea ducem,
sentences.l:
Rumour flies that driven from the kingdoms of his fathers
Idomeneus the leader had gone,
sentences.i: Rumour flies that Idomeneus, the leader, driven from his father's kingdom, has withdrawn,
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'Fama volat' is 'rumour flies', and what follows is an accusative and infinitive: 'Idomenea ducem… cessisse', 'that the leader Idomeneus had withdrawn'. 'pulsum' is the perfect passive participle of 'pello', 'driven out', agreeing with 'ducem'. 'Idomenea' is the Greek accusative of 'Idomeneus'. The tradition (not in Homer) was that the Cretan king, back from Troy, was driven out of Crete.

sentences.t:
desertaque litora Cretae
hoste vacare domos, sedesque adstare relictas.
sentences.l:
and the deserted shores of Crete,
the houses to be free of the enemy, and the abandoned seats to stand ready.
sentences.i: and that the shores of Crete lay deserted, her houses free of any foe, her abandoned dwellings standing ready.
sentences.n: The accusative and infinitive goes on piece by piece: 'desertaque litora Cretae' (the shores of Crete deserted, with no verb of its own), 'hoste vacare domos' and 'sedes adstare relictas'. The infinitives are 'vacare' and 'adstare' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'astare'). The subjects are 'litora' (with 'deserta'), 'domos' and 'sedes'; for 'domos' the Latin Library prints 'domum', a genitive plural, which would change the construction. 'hoste' is an ablative of separation with 'vacare', 'be free of, be empty of'. 'adstare relictas' is 'stand there, left behind', that is, ready to be occupied.

sentences.t: Linquimus Ortygiae portus, pelagoque volamus,
sentences.l: We leave the harbours of Ortygia, and over the sea we fly,
sentences.i: We leave the harbours of Ortygia and fly over the sea,
sentences.n: The narration returns to Aeneas, with a narrative present, 'Linquimus', 'volamus'. 'Ortygiae' is Delos, the island of the oracle, one of whose names was Ortygia. 'portus' is an accusative plural in -us. 'pelago' is an ablative of route or means, 'over the sea'. 'volamus' is the usual poetic word for a swift voyage.

sentences.t:
bacchatamque iugis Naxon viridemque Donysam,
Olearon, niveamque Paron, sparsasque per aequor
Cycladas, et crebris legimus freta consita terris.
sentences.l:
and Naxos revelled on its ridges and green Donysa,
Olearos, and snowy Paros, and scattered over the sea
Cyclades, and we skim the straits sown with crowded lands.
sentences.i: We pass Naxos, with Bacchic revels on its ridges, green Donysa, Olearos, snow-white Paros, and the Cyclades scattered across the water; and we skim the seas planted thick with lands.
sentences.n: A catalogue of islands in the Aegean, all objects of 'legimus' (the verb is held to the end of the list). 'bacchatam… iugis' is a perfect passive participle of the deponent 'bacchor', 'revelled', used passively: Naxos was Dionysus' island. 'Donysam' is Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library prints 'Donusam'). 'Olearon' and 'Paron' are Greek accusatives of 'Olearos' and 'Paros'. 'niveam' is 'snow-white', for the marble. 'Cycladas' is the Greek accusative plural, 'the Cyclades', the circle of islands round Delos (Greek 'kyklos'). 'legimus' is the present of 'lego', here 'skirt, pass along'. 'consita' is the perfect passive participle of 'consero', 'sown, planted', a bold metaphor for islands scattered like seeds; the Latin Library prints 'concita', 'stirred', a different word. 'crebris… terris' is an ablative with 'consita', 'sown with crowded lands'.

sentences.t: Nauticus exoritur vario certamine clamor;
sentences.l: A nautical shout rises in varied rivalry;
sentences.i: A shout from the sailors goes up as each crew vies with another;
sentences.n: 'Nauticus' is an adjective, 'of sailors', agreeing with 'clamor'. 'exoritur' is the present of the deponent 'exorior'. 'vario certamine' is an ablative of manner or cause, 'in varied contention', the crews shouting in rivalry with one another.

sentences.t: hortantur socii:
sentences.l: the comrades urge:
sentences.i: the comrades cheer us on:
sentences.n: 'hortantur' is the present of the deponent 'hortor', 'urge on, encourage'. 'socii' are the crew, 'companions'. The colon introduces the cry.

sentences.t: “Cretam proavosque petamus!”
sentences.l: “Let us seek Crete and our forefathers!”
sentences.i: “To Crete, to our forefathers!”
sentences.n: The sailors' cry, with the opening “ and the closing ”, a single line. 'petamus' is a hortatory subjunctive. 'proavos' means 'forefathers', specifically the remote ancestors; the sailors have understood Anchises' reading of the oracle.

sentences.t:
Prosequitur surgens a puppi ventus euntis
et tandem antiquis Curetum adlabimur oris.
sentences.l:
Follows, rising from the stern, a wind, us as we go,
and at last to the ancient shores of the Curetes we glide.
sentences.i: A wind rising behind us follows us on our way, and at last we glide to the ancient shores of the Curetes.
sentences.n: 'Prosequitur' is the present of the deponent 'prosequor', 'follows (and speeds)'. 'surgens a puppi ventus' is 'a wind rising from the stern', a following wind, and 'euntis' is an accusative plural in -is of the participle, 'us as we go'. 'Curetum' is the genitive plural of 'Curetes', a Greek third-declension name (-um, not -orum): in the legend the Curetes were the old inhabitants of Crete, the guardians of the infant Jupiter. 'adlabimur' is the present of the deponent 'adlabor', 'glide to', governing a dative: 'antiquis… oris'.

sentences.t: Ergo avidus muros optatae molior urbis,
sentences.l: Therefore eagerly I build the walls of the wished-for city,
sentences.i: So I eagerly set about the walls of the city I had hoped for,
sentences.n: 'Ergo' is 'so, therefore'. 'avidus' is nominative singular, 'eager'. 'molior' is the present of the deponent 'molior', 'toil at, build'. 'optatae… urbis' is 'of the desired city'.

sentences.t:
Pergameamque voco, et laetam cognomine gentem
hortor amare focos arcemque attollere tectis.
sentences.l:
and I call it Pergamum, and the people glad at the name
I urge to love their hearths and to raise a citadel with roofs.
sentences.i: I call it Pergamum, and urge the people, glad of the name, to love their hearths and to raise a citadel with its roofs.
sentences.n: 'Pergameam' is an adjective used as a noun ('urbem' understood from 'urbis'), the object of 'voco', 'I call'; the name comes from Pergamum, Troy's citadel. 'laetam cognomine gentem' is 'the people glad in the name', and 'cognomine' is an ablative of cause. 'hortor' is followed by two infinitives ('amare', 'attollere'), the construction used by poets where prose uses 'ut' and the subjunctive. 'tectis' is an ablative of means or accompaniment: the citadel is raised 'with roofs', that is, with buildings.

sentences.t: Iamque fere sicco subductae litore puppes;
sentences.l: And now almost on dry shore the ships had been drawn up;
sentences.i: Now the ships were all but drawn up on the dry shore;
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'subductae' is the perfect participle of 'subduco', 'drawn up', the usual way of beaching a ship. 'sicco… litore' is an ablative of place where, 'on the dry shore', that is, above the waterline. 'fere' is 'almost'. Greenough prints no verb ('erant' is understood), and this and the next two clauses are a run of descriptive clauses.

sentences.t: conubiis arvisque novis operata iuventus;
sentences.l: with marriages and new fields the young men busy;
sentences.i: the young men were busy with weddings and new farmland;
sentences.n: 'operata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'operor', 'be busy with', which takes a dative ('conubiis arvisque novis', a form identical with the ablative). The perfect participle of a deponent has an active sense, as here. 'iuventus' is a collective noun, 'the young men'. 'conubiis' is Greenough's spelling of 'connubiis', 'marriages'.

sentences.t: iura domosque dabam:
sentences.l: laws and homes I was giving:
sentences.i: I was giving them laws and houses,
sentences.n: 'iura domosque dabam' is the imperfect, 'I was giving', an action under way. The colon prepares for the interruption that follows with 'cum'. 'iura' means 'laws' and 'domos' means 'houses', both objects of 'dabam'.

sentences.t:
subito cum tabida membris,
corrupto caeli tractu, miserandaque venit
arboribusque satisque lues et letifer annus.
sentences.l:
when suddenly, wasting for bodies,
with the region of the sky corrupted, and pitiable came
to both trees and crops a plague, and a deadly year.
sentences.i: when suddenly, from a tainted sky, a wasting plague fell on their limbs, pitiful for trees and crops alike — a deadly season.
sentences.n: 'cum' with the indicative ('venit') is the 'cum inversum': 'when suddenly came'. 'tabida' and 'miseranda' describe 'lues' (singular, 'plague'); 'letifer' goes with 'annus'. 'tabida' is 'wasting' and 'membris' is a dative of the sufferers, 'for the limbs, bodies'. 'corrupto caeli tractu' is an ablative absolute, 'the region of the sky being corrupted', the air tainted. 'miseranda' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be pitied', and 'arboribus satisque' is a dative of the thing affected, 'for trees and crops' ('satis' is the dative or ablative plural of 'sata', 'crops'). The verb 'venit' is singular, agreeing with the first subject, 'lues'; 'letifer annus' is a second subject added.

sentences.t:
Linquebant dulcis animas, aut aegra trahebant
corpora;
sentences.l:
They left sweet lives, or sick were dragging
their bodies;
sentences.i: Men gave up sweet life, or dragged on with sickened bodies;
sentences.n: 'Linquebant' is the imperfect, 'they were leaving', an unstated 'they' being the people. 'dulcis animas' is an accusative plural in -is, 'sweet lives'. 'aegra' agrees with 'corpora', which is held over into the next line. 'trahebant' is 'were dragging', they dragged themselves about sick.

sentences.t: tum sterilis exurere Sirius agros;
sentences.l: then Sirius to scorch the barren fields;
sentences.i: then Sirius scorched the barren fields;
sentences.n: 'exurere' is a historic infinitive, an infinitive used as if it were a past tense with a subject in the nominative ('Sirius'); it gives a sudden, quick sense, and Virgil uses it for vivid narrative. Sirius, the Dog Star, rises in the hottest part of summer and was believed to bring drought and disease. 'tum' is 'then'. 'sterilis… agros' is an accusative plural in -is: 'the barren fields'.

sentences.t: arebant herbae, et victum seges aegra negabat.
sentences.l: the grasses were withering, and the sick crop denied food.
sentences.i: the grass withered, and the sickly crop refused food.
sentences.n: 'arebant' is the imperfect of 'areo', 'be dry, wither'. 'victum' is 'food', the object of 'negabat', 'denied'; 'seges aegra' is 'the sick crop', the standing corn. After the infinitive of the last unit, the narrative is back in ordinary imperfects.

sentences.t:
Rursus ad oraclum Ortygiae Phoebumque remenso
hortatur pater ire mari, veniamque precari:
sentences.l:
Again to the oracle of Ortygia and to Phoebus, retraced,
urges the father to go by sea, and to beg for favour:
sentences.i: Again my father bids me retrace the sea to the oracle of Ortygia and to Phoebus, and beg his favour:
sentences.n: 'oraclum' is a contracted form of 'oraculum' (the unstressed vowel dropped, as often in verse). 'Rursus' is 'again', the Trojans having consulted the oracle once already. 'remenso… mari' is an ablative absolute, 'the sea having been measured again', in its passive sense. 'hortatur' governs the infinitives 'ire' and 'precari' (the poetic construction, with 'me' understood). 'pater' is Anchises. 'veniam' is 'favour, grace, pardon'. The colon introduces the matters to be asked.

sentences.t: quam fessis finem rebus ferat;
sentences.l: to what end for weary affairs he may bring;
sentences.i: what end he will bring to our wearied fortunes;
sentences.n: The next three clauses are indirect questions, so their verbs are subjunctive; they depend on the thought of asking implied in 'precari'. 'quam… finem' separates the adjective from its noun (hyperbaton). 'fessis rebus' is a dative of advantage, 'for our wearied fortunes'; 'ferat' is the present subjunctive of 'fero', 'bring', the god being the subject.

sentences.t:
unde laborum
temptare auxilium iubeat;
sentences.l:
from where of toils the help to try
he may bid;
sentences.i: where he will bid us look for help in our toils;
sentences.n: 'unde' is 'from what quarter'. 'laborum' is a genitive with 'auxilium', 'help in the toils' (or 'against'). 'temptare' is the infinitive after 'iubeat', 'he may bid us attempt', with 'nos' understood. 'iubeat' is the present subjunctive of an indirect question.

sentences.t: quo vertere cursus.
sentences.l: to where to turn our courses.
sentences.i: and where to turn our course.
sentences.n: 'quo' is 'to what place'; 'iubeat' is understood from the last clause, and 'vertere' is the infinitive. 'cursus' is an accusative plural (the fourth declension), 'courses'. The last of three questions, ellipsis keeping the series quick.

sentences.t: Nox erat, et terris animalia somnus habebat:
sentences.l: It was night, and sleep held living things on the lands:
sentences.i: It was night, and sleep held every living creature on the earth:
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'Nox erat' is the scene-setting formula of an epic night. 'animalia' is a neuter plural noun, 'living things', and 'terris' is an ablative of place where, without a preposition, 'over the lands'. 'habebat' means 'held'. The colon introduces what Aeneas saw in his sleep.

sentences.t: effigies sacrae divom Phrygiique Penates,
sentences.l: the sacred images of the gods and the Phrygian Penates,
sentences.i: the sacred images of the gods, the Trojan Penates,
sentences.n: 'effigies… Penates' is the subject, picked up by 'visi' (line 150), which is masculine and so agrees with 'Penates'. 'divom' is the old genitive plural for 'divorum' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'diuum'). The Penates were the Roman household gods, here the Trojan images of the home gods that Aeneas brought from Troy. 'Phrygii' means 'Trojan'.

sentences.t:
quos mecum a Troia mediisque ex ignibus urbis
extuleram,
sentences.l:
whom with me from Troy and from the midst of the city's fires
I had carried out,
sentences.i: whom I had carried with me from Troy and from the midst of the city's fires,
sentences.n: 'quos' is the relative pronoun of a plain relative clause: the antecedent is 'Penates'. 'extuleram' is the pluperfect of 'effero', 'carry out'. The rescue is told in Book II (Hector's ghost gave them to Aeneas). 'mediis ex ignibus urbis' is 'from the midst of the city's fires' (the adjective 'mediis' agrees with 'ignibus').

sentences.t:
visi ante oculos adstare iacentis
in somnis, multo manifesti lumine,
sentences.l:
seemed before the eyes to stand of one lying
in sleep, plain in abundant light,
sentences.i: seemed to stand before my eyes as I lay in sleep, plain to see in a flood of light,
sentences.n: 'visi' is the nominative plural of the perfect participle of 'video' used passively, 'seemed' (the subject being 'effigies… Penates'); 'adstare' is the infinitive that goes with it (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'astare'). 'iacentis' is the genitive singular of 'iacens', 'of one lying', agreeing with an unstated 'mei' ('my'): so 'before the eyes of me lying', a Latin way of saying 'as I lay'. 'in somnis' is 'in sleep' (the plural is standard). 'multo manifesti lumine' means 'clearly seen in abundant light': 'manifesti' agrees with 'visi'.

sentences.t:
qua se
plena per insertas fundebat luna fenestras;
sentences.l:
where itself
the full moon through the inset windows was pouring;
sentences.i: where the full moon was pouring through the windows let into the wall;
sentences.n: 'qua' is a relative adverb, 'where, by which way'. 'plena… luna' is the full moon, and 'fundebat' means 'was pouring'. 'se' is the reflexive: the moon was pouring itself, its light, in. 'insertas fenestras' means 'windows set into' the wall (the perfect passive participle of 'insero').

sentences.t: tum sic adfari et curas his demere dictis:
sentences.l: then so to speak and to take cares away with these words:
sentences.i: then to speak thus, and take my cares away with such words:
sentences.n: The last two infinitives depend on 'visi' in the same way: they seemed 'adfari', 'to address' (the infinitive of the deponent 'adfor'), and 'demere', 'to take away'. 'his… dictis' is an ablative of means, 'with these words'. The colon introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
“Quod tibi delato Ortygiam dicturus Apollo est,
hic canit, et tua nos en ultro ad limina mittit.
sentences.l:
“What to you, brought to Ortygia, Apollo is about to say,
here he sings, and us to your threshold, see, of his own accord sends.
sentences.i: “What Apollo would tell you if you were carried to Ortygia, he declares here, and see, he sends us of his own will to your very door.
sentences.n: The Penates' speech begins, with the opening “; it ends at 171. 'Quod' is a relative: 'what' (the antecedent 'id' is understood, object of 'canit'). 'dicturus… est' is the future participle with 'est', 'is about to say'. 'tibi delato Ortygiam' is a dative with the perfect participle of 'defero' used conditionally, 'if you were brought to Ortygia'; 'Ortygiam' is an accusative of motion, with no preposition, as with names of islands. 'hic' means 'here'. 'canit' is the present of 'cano', 'sings, utters' (oracles and seers 'sing'). 'en' means 'see!'. 'ultro' means 'of his own accord'.

sentences.t:
Nos te, Dardania incensa, tuaque arma secuti,
nos tumidum sub te permensi classibus aequor,
sentences.l:
We, you, Dardania burned, and your arms having followed,
we the swelling sea under you having crossed with fleets,
sentences.i: We who followed you and your arms when Dardania burned, we who crossed the swollen sea under your command with fleets,
sentences.n: 'Dardania incensa' is an ablative absolute, 'Dardania being burned'. 'secuti' and 'permensi' are perfect participles of the deponents 'sequor' and 'permetior', so 'having followed' and 'having crossed', and both agree with 'nos' (anaphora of 'nos… nos'). 'sub te' is 'under you', under your leadership. 'tumidum… aequor' is 'the swelling sea'. 'classibus' is an ablative of means or accompaniment, 'with fleets'. The long subject waits for its verb, 'tollemus', in the next line.

sentences.t: idem venturos tollemus in astra nepotes,
sentences.l: we the same will raise to the stars your descendants to come,
sentences.i: we, the same gods, shall lift your coming descendants to the stars
sentences.n: 'idem' is the nominative plural masculine of 'idem', 'the same' (the same ones who followed you will do this). 'tollemus in astra' is 'we shall raise to the stars', a promise of glory for the race. 'venturos… nepotes' means 'descendants who are to come', with 'venturos' the future participle of 'venio'.

sentences.t: imperiumque urbi dabimus:
sentences.l: and empire to the city we shall give:
sentences.i: and give empire to their city.
sentences.n: 'imperium' is 'empire, rule', and 'urbi' is a dative, 'to the city', Rome. 'dabimus' is a future. The colon here introduces the command that follows.

sentences.t:
tu moenia magnis
magna para, longumque fugae ne linque laborem.
sentences.l:
you walls for the great
great prepare, and the long toil of flight do not leave.
sentences.i: You, for the great ones, prepare great walls; and do not give up the long labour of your flight.
sentences.n: 'tu moenia magnis magna para' sets 'magnis' and 'magna' side by side for emphasis, with 'moenia' between the pair of 'tu… para'. 'magnis' is a dative, 'for the great (the great descendants)'. 'para' is the imperative of 'paro'. 'ne linque' is a negative imperative made with 'ne' and the imperative, a poetic usage (prose would say 'noli relinquere'). 'longum… laborem' is 'the long toil'; 'fugae' is a genitive, 'of flight, exile'.

sentences.t: Mutandae sedes:
sentences.l: To be changed are the seats:
sentences.i: You must change your dwelling-place.
sentences.n: 'Mutandae sedes' is an elliptical gerundive, 'sunt' left out: the seats are 'to be changed', that is, 'must be changed'. The colon introduces the reason.

sentences.t:
non haec tibi litora suasit
Delius, aut Cretae iussit considere Apollo.
sentences.l:
not these shores to you has urged
the Delian, or to settle on Crete has bid, Apollo.
sentences.i: It was not these shores that the Delian counselled you to find, nor did Apollo tell you to settle in Crete.
sentences.n: 'Delius… Apollo' is split by the rest of the sentence (hyperbaton): 'Delius' means 'the god of Delos'. 'suasit' is the perfect of 'suadeo', 'advise', governing an accusative ('haec litora') in this poetic use; 'iussit' is 'ordered', with the infinitive 'considere'. 'Cretae' is a locative, 'in Crete'. The Penates say that the oracle did not point to Crete: Aeneas had misread it.

sentences.t: Est locus, Hesperiam Grai cognomine dicunt,
sentences.l: There is a place, Hesperia the Greeks by name call it,
sentences.i: There is a land the Greeks call Hesperia by name,
sentences.n: 'Est locus' is an opening formula for a description. 'Hesperiam… dicunt' is 'they call it Hesperia' (the 'Western land', from the Greek 'hespera', evening); 'cognomine' is an ablative of the name. 'Grai' is the contracted form of 'Graii', the Greeks (two syllables in the verse).

sentences.t: terra antiqua, potens armis atque ubere glaebae;
sentences.l: a land ancient, mighty in arms and in the richness of soil;
sentences.i: an ancient land, strong in arms and in the richness of its soil;
sentences.n: 'terra antiqua' is in apposition to 'locus'. 'potens' takes the ablative 'armis' ('strong in arms'); 'ubere' is the ablative of the noun 'uber', 'richness', with 'glaebae' as its genitive, 'in richness of soil'. The Latin gives a pair of strengths, war and farming.

sentences.t: Oenotri coluere viri;
sentences.l: the Oenotrian men have lived there;
sentences.i: Oenotrian men once lived there;
sentences.n: 'Oenotri' is the Oenotrians, an early people of southern Italy. 'coluere' is 'coluerunt' (-ere = -erunt, you'll see this constantly), 'inhabited'. 'viri' is in apposition.

sentences.t:
nunc fama minores
Italiam dixisse ducis de nomine gentem:
sentences.l:
now rumour that the younger ones
Italy have called the nation from the name of the leader:
sentences.i: now the report is that their later descendants have named the nation Italy after their leader:
sentences.n: 'est' is understood: 'now (there is) the report that…' and the accusative and infinitive follows: 'minores… dixisse… gentem', 'that the younger folk have called the nation'. 'minores' means 'those who came later'. 'Italiam' is the predicate accusative, 'Italy', 'gentem' being the object. 'ducis de nomine' means 'from the name of the leader' (Italus, by the ancient tradition). The colon prepares for the claim.

sentences.t: hae nobis propriae sedes;
sentences.l: these are our own seats;
sentences.i: This is our own home;
sentences.n: 'hae nobis propriae sedes' has 'sunt' understood, and 'nobis' is a dative of possession, 'ours' (as in the pilot's 'sunt mihi'), and 'propriae' means 'our very own, permanent'.

sentences.t:
hinc Dardanus ortus,
Iasiusque pater, genus a quo principe nostrum.
sentences.l:
from here Dardanus rose,
and father Iasius, from whom as founder our race.
sentences.i: From here Dardanus sprang, and father Iasius, from whom, as first of the line, our race descends.
sentences.n: 'hinc' means 'from here', from Italy; Virgil here follows the tradition by which Dardanus (founder of the Trojan royal line) came from Italy, from Corythus in Etruria. 'ortus' is the perfect participle of 'orior', 'risen, born', with 'est' omitted. 'Iasius' is Dardanus' brother (a mythical ancestor), and 'pater' is 'forefather'. The Latin 'a quo principe' means 'from whom as first author' (an ablative of origin), and 'genus… nostrum' is the subject, 'est' left out.

sentences.t:
Surge age, et haec laetus longaevo dicta parenti
haud dubitanda refer:
sentences.l:
Rise up, and these words, glad, to your aged father
not to be doubted, carry back:
sentences.i: Rise now, and gladly take these words, which are not to be doubted, to your aged father:
sentences.n: 'Surge age' means 'up, then!' ('age' is a particle of urging). 'haec… dicta' means 'these words', the object of 'refer' (the imperative of 'refero'), with 'haud dubitanda' (a gerundive, 'not to be doubted') agreeing with it. 'longaevo… parenti' is a dative, 'to your long-lived father', Anchises. The colon introduces the message.

sentences.t:
Corythum terrasque requirat
Ausonias;
sentences.l:
let him seek Corythus and the lands
Ausonian;
sentences.i: let him look for Corythus and the Ausonian lands;
sentences.n: 'requirat' is a jussive subjunctive in the reported message, 'let him seek'. 'Corythum' is the Etruscan city of Corythus, the home of Dardanus in the tradition; 'Ausonias' is an adjective, 'Ausonian', that is, Italian (from the Ausones, an old people of the peninsula). The instruction does not say Italy by name.

sentences.t: Dictaea negat tibi Iuppiter arva.”
sentences.l: the Dictaean fields Jupiter denies you.”
sentences.i: Jupiter does not grant you the fields of Dicte.”
sentences.n: 'Dictaea… arva' means 'the Dictaean fields', Crete, from Mount Dicte there. 'negat' means 'refuses', and 'tibi' is a dative. The closing ” ends the Penates' speech, which opened at 154.

sentences.t: Talibus attonitus visis et voce deorum—
sentences.l: By such visions astonished and by the voice of the gods —
sentences.i: Stunned by such sights and by the voice of the gods —
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'attonitus' is the perfect participle of 'attono', 'thunderstruck, stunned'. It is nominative and masculine and belongs with the 'I' of 'corripio' in line 176; the dash opens a parenthesis in which Aeneas insists that the vision was real, and the sentence resumes after it. 'Talibus… visis' is an ablative of cause, 'by such sights'.

sentences.t:
nec sopor illud erat, sed coram adgnoscere voltus
velatasque comas praesentiaque ora videbar;
sentences.l:
nor was that sleep, but face to face to know the looks
and veiled hair and present faces I seemed;
sentences.i: It was not sleep: face to face I seemed to know their looks, their veiled hair, their faces present before me;
sentences.n: The parenthesis. 'nec sopor illud erat' is 'that was not sleep'. 'videbar' is the passive of 'video', 'I seemed', with the infinitive 'adgnoscere' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'agnoscere'), 'to recognise'. 'coram' means 'face to face'. 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus'. 'velatas comas' means 'covered hair', hair covered with a veil or bound with a fillet, as for a sacred figure. 'praesentia ora' means 'faces present', real, before him. The semicolon is Greenough's.

sentences.t:
tum gelidus toto manabat corpore sudor
corripio e stratis corpus, tendoque supinas
ad caelum cum voce manus, et munera libo
intemerata focis.
sentences.l:
then a cold sweat ran down over all my body
I snatch my body from the bedclothes, and I stretch upturned
to heaven with a cry my hands, and gifts I pour out
undefiled on the hearths.
sentences.i: Then a cold sweat poured over my whole body; I snatch myself from my bedding, stretch my upturned hands to heaven, with a cry, and pour out unspoiled offerings on the hearth.
sentences.n: Greenough prints no stop after 'sudor', and the line runs straight into the main verbs; the English has to supply one. 'gelidus… sudor' is 'cold sweat', and 'manabat' is the imperfect of 'mano', 'flow'. 'corripio… corpus' is the present, 'I snatch up (my body)', 'e stratis' means 'from the bedclothes'. 'tendo… supinas… manus' means 'I stretch my upturned hands' (palms up in prayer). 'libo' is the present of 'libo', 'I pour as a libation'. 'munera… intemerata' means 'unspoiled gifts', pure libations. 'focis' is a dative or ablative, 'on the hearths' (the household altars).

sentences.t:
Perfecto laetus honore
Anchisen facio certum, remque ordine pando.
sentences.l:
When the honour was done, glad,
I make Anchises sure, and the matter in order I lay open.
sentences.i: When the rite was done, I gladly informed Anchises, and laid out the whole matter in order.
sentences.n: 'Perfecto… honore' is an ablative absolute, 'the offering having been completed'. 'facio certum' means 'I make (Anchises) sure', that is, 'I inform'. 'Anchisen' is the Greek accusative of 'Anchises'. 'pando' is the present of 'pando', 'spread out, lay open'. The tense is the narrative present.

sentences.t: Adgnovit prolem ambiguam geminosque parentes,
sentences.l: He recognised the doubtful stock and the twin parents,
sentences.i: He saw that the line of their race was twofold, and the parents twin,
sentences.n: 'Adgnovit' (Greenough's spelling; the Latin Library prints 'agnouit') is the perfect of 'adgnosco'. 'prolem ambiguam' means 'the ambiguous, doubtful stock' and 'geminos parentes' means 'the two ancestors'; the Latin Library prints 'parentis', the same accusative plural in the -is spelling, which does not change the sense. Anchises sees that the Trojans have two founders (Teucer, from Crete, and Dardanus, from Italy), and has mixed them up.

sentences.t: seque novo veterum deceptum errore locorum.
sentences.l: and himself by a new error of the old places deceived.
sentences.i: and that he had been deceived by a fresh error about the places of old.
sentences.n: The accusative and infinitive continues: 'se… deceptum (esse)'. 'novo… errore' is an ablative of means, 'by a fresh mistake', and 'veterum… locorum' is a genitive, 'about the old places'. The error is that he took Crete to be the original homeland.

sentences.t: Tum memorat:
sentences.l: Then he recalls:
sentences.i: Then he says:
sentences.n: 'memorat' is the present of 'memoro', 'recall, relate', here the verb that introduces his speech. The colon introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
“Nate, Iliacis exercite fatis,
sola mihi talis casus Cassandra canebat.
sentences.l:
“Son, harried by Ilian fates,
Cassandra alone to me such events used to sing.
sentences.i: “My son, tried so hard by the fates of Ilium, only Cassandra used to foretell such happenings to me.
sentences.n: Anchises' second speech begins, with the opening “; it runs to 188. 'Nate' is the vocative of 'natus', 'son'. 'exercite' is the vocative of the perfect participle of 'exerceo', 'harried, driven', with 'Iliacis… fatis' as an ablative of means. 'sola… Cassandra' is the subject, with 'mihi' a dative of the person told. 'canebat' is the imperfect of 'cano', repeated action. Cassandra, Priam's daughter, was gifted with prophecy by Apollo and cursed never to be believed.

sentences.t:
Nunc repeto haec generi portendere debita nostro,
et saepe Hesperiam, saepe Itala regna vocare.
sentences.l:
Now I recall her to portend these things, owed to our race,
and often Hesperia, often Italian realms to call.
sentences.i: Now I remember that these things were foretold as owed to our house, and that she often spoke of Hesperia, often of the Italian kingdoms.
sentences.n: 'repeto' is 'I call to mind again'. 'portendere', 'to portend', is an infinitive after 'repeto' whose subject, Cassandra, is left unexpressed ('I recall her portending'); 'haec' is its object, and 'debita' is 'owed', 'due', in the sense of 'destined', agreeing with 'haec'. 'generi nostro' is a dative, 'to our stock'. 'vocare' is a second infinitive of the same construction, with the same unexpressed subject, Cassandra, 'she called'; 'saepe… saepe' repeats the word.

sentences.t:
Sed quis ad Hesperiae venturos litora Teucros
crederet, aut quem tum vates Cassandra moveret?
sentences.l:
But who would have believed that to the shores of Hesperia Teucrians would come,
or whom then would the prophetess Cassandra have moved?
sentences.i: But who would have believed that Teucrians were to come to the shores of Hesperia, or whom would the seer Cassandra then have moved?
sentences.n: Both clauses are rhetorical questions in the imperfect subjunctive, 'crederet… moveret', 'who would have believed?' (a potential of the past). 'venturos… Teucros' is an accusative and infinitive, 'that the Teucrians would come' ('esse' is understood). 'vates' is 'seer, prophetess'. The questions say that nobody believed Cassandra.

sentences.t: Cedamus Phoebo, et moniti meliora sequamur.”
sentences.l: Let us yield to Phoebus, and warned the better follow.”
sentences.i: Let us yield to Phoebus, and, now warned, follow the better course.”
sentences.n: The speech ends with the closing ” after a hortatory pair. 'Cedamus' and 'sequamur' are hortatory subjunctives, 'let us yield', 'let us follow'. 'Phoebo' is a dative with 'cedo'. 'moniti' is the nominative plural of the perfect participle of 'moneo', 'warned', and 'meliora' is the neuter plural of 'melior', 'the better things'.

sentences.t: Sic ait, et cuncti dicto paremus ovantes.
sentences.l: So he says, and all to his word we obey rejoicing.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and we all obeyed his word with joy.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait' closes the speech, as 'Sic fatus' did earlier. 'dicto' is a dative with the verb 'paremus' (from 'pareo', 'obey', which takes the dative). 'ovantes' is a present participle, 'exulting, rejoicing' (from 'ovo'; the word elsewhere describes a triumph).

sentences.t:
Hanc quoque deserimus sedem, paucisque relictis
vela damus, vastumque cava trabe currimus aequor.
sentences.l:
This seat too we leave, and a few left behind
sails we give, and the vast sea with hollow beam we run.
sentences.i: We leave this place as well, with a few left behind, and spread our sails, and run over the vast sea in our hollow timbers.
sentences.n: 'Hanc quoque… sedem' is 'this seat also' (the Cretan settlement). 'paucis relictis' is an ablative absolute, 'a few being left behind', some who stayed. 'vela damus' is 'we give the sails (to the winds)', a standard phrase. 'cava trabe' is 'with hollow timber', the ship (trabs is 'beam', the part for the whole), an ablative of means. 'currimus aequor' is 'we run the sea', where the accusative 'aequor' is a poetic object of 'currimus' (as if the sea were the course run).

sentences.t:
Postquam altum tenuere rates, nec iam amplius ullae
adparent terrae, caelum undique et undique pontus,
sentences.l:
After the deep the ships held, and no longer any more
appear lands, sky on all sides and on all sides sea,
sentences.i: After the ships had gained the deep, and no more land at all was to be seen, but sky on every side and sea on every side,
sentences.n: New paragraph. 'Postquam' with the perfect 'tenuere' (-ere = -erunt) gives 'after they held'. 'altum' is 'the deep, the high sea'. 'nec iam amplius ullae adparent terrae' is 'no lands any longer appear', with Greenough's spelling 'adparent' (the Latin Library prints 'apparent'). 'caelum undique et undique pontus' has no verb: a vivid fragment ('erat' is understood), with the repeated 'undique'. The comma leads to the main clause.

sentences.t:
tum mihi caeruleus supra caput adstitit imber,
noctem hiememque ferens, et inhorruit unda tenebris.
sentences.l:
then to me dark blue above my head stood a rain-cloud,
bringing night and storm, and the wave bristled with darkness.
sentences.i: then a dark rain-cloud halted above my head, bringing night and foul weather, and the water shuddered under the gloom.
sentences.n: 'tum' is the main clause that 'postquam' prepared. 'mihi' is a dative of the person concerned ('for me'), and 'supra caput' is 'above my head'. 'caeruleus… imber' means 'the dark blue rain-cloud'. 'adstitit' is the perfect of 'adsto' (the Latin Library prints 'astitit'), 'stood by'. 'ferens' is a present participle, 'bringing', with the two objects 'noctem hiememque'. 'inhorruit' is the perfect of 'inhorreo' (or 'inhorresco'), 'bristle, shudder'; 'unda' is the sea's surface, and 'tenebris' an ablative of cause or means, 'with darkness'.

sentences.t:
Continuo venti volvunt mare, magnaque surgunt
aequora;
sentences.l:
At once the winds roll the sea, and great
waters rise;
sentences.i: At once the winds heave up the sea, and great waves rise;
sentences.n: 'Continuo' is 'at once, immediately'. 'volvunt' is 'roll, churn'. 'magna… aequora' is a framing of the verb by an adjective and noun, 'great… waters'; 'aequora' is the plural of 'aequor', 'surface of the sea'. A semicolon marks the pause.

sentences.t: dispersi iactamur gurgite vasto;
sentences.l: scattered we are tossed on the vast flood;
sentences.i: scattered, we are tossed on the vast gulf;
sentences.n: 'dispersi' is the nominative plural of the perfect participle of 'dispergo', 'scattered'. 'iactamur' is the present passive of 'iacto', 'we are tossed about'. 'gurgite vasto' is an ablative of place where, 'on the vast whirlpool, gulf'.

sentences.t:
involvere diem nimbi, et nox umida caelum
abstulit;
sentences.l:
the rain clouds have wrapped up the day, and wet night the sky
has taken away;
sentences.i: storm-clouds have wrapped up the day, and damp night has snatched the heavens away;
sentences.n: 'involvere' is the perfect 'involverunt' (-ere = -erunt), 'enveloped', with 'diem' as its object and 'nimbi' as subject. 'nox umida' is 'wet night', with 'caelum' as the object of 'abstulit', the perfect of 'aufero', 'take away'. The perfects give the sudden effect.

sentences.t: ingeminant abruptis nubibus ignes.
sentences.l: the fires redouble from the burst clouds.
sentences.i: flashes of fire come thick and double from the riven clouds.
sentences.n: 'ingeminant' is the present of 'ingemino', 'redouble, repeat', here the lightning flashing again and again; 'ignes' is its subject. 'abruptis nubibus' is an ablative of source or separation, 'from clouds torn open'.

sentences.t: Excutimur cursu, et caecis erramus in undis.
sentences.l: We are shaken from our course, and wander in blind waves.
sentences.i: We are shaken off our course, and stray over blind waters.
sentences.n: 'Excutimur' is the present passive of 'excutio', 'shake out', 'cursu' being an ablative of separation. 'caecis… in undis' means 'in blind waves', waves where no one can see, a transferred epithet. 'erramus' means 'we wander'.

sentences.t:
Ipse diem noctemque negat discernere caelo,
nec meminisse viae media Palinurus in unda.
sentences.l:
Himself the day and the night denies he can tell apart in the sky,
nor to remember the way in mid wave, Palinurus.
sentences.i: Palinurus himself declares he cannot tell day from night in the sky, nor recall the way amid the waves.
sentences.n: 'Ipse… Palinurus' frames the sentence (hyperbaton): Palinurus is Aeneas' helmsman, and 'ipse' stresses that even the expert is lost. 'negat' means 'he says that he cannot', governing the infinitives 'discernere' and 'meminisse' ('negat' = 'dicit non'). 'caelo' is an ablative of place where. 'meminisse' (the perfect infinitive, with present sense) takes a genitive, 'viae', 'of the way'. 'media… in unda' means 'in the middle of the water'.

sentences.t:
Tris adeo incertos caeca caligine soles
erramus pelago, totidem sine sidere noctes.
sentences.l:
Three whole uncertain suns in blind darkness
we wander on the sea, as many nights without a star.
sentences.i: For three whole days, uncertain, in blinding gloom, we wander over the sea, and as many nights with no star.
sentences.n: 'Tris' is an accusative plural in -is (for 'tres'), agreeing with 'soles'; 'adeo' adds emphasis, 'for three whole days'. The accusatives 'soles' and 'noctes' express duration of time. 'incertos' agrees with 'soles' (a transferred epithet: it is the sailors who are uncertain). 'caeca caligine' is an ablative of means or manner, 'in blind mist'. 'totidem' means 'just as many'. 'sine sidere' means 'without a star'.

sentences.t:
Quarto terra die primum se attollere tandem
visa, aperire procul montis, ac volvere fumum.
sentences.l:
On the fourth day land first itself to raise at last
was seen, to open mountains far off, and to roll smoke.
sentences.i: On the fourth day land at last seemed first to lift itself, to open out mountains in the distance and to roll up smoke.
sentences.n: 'Quarto… die' is an ablative of time when. 'terra… visa' is 'the land was seen to', 'visa (est)', the perfect passive of 'video' in the sense 'seemed'; it is followed by three infinitives ('attollere', 'aperire', 'volvere'). 'se attollere' means 'to raise itself'. 'aperire… montis' is 'to open out mountains', to reveal them (an accusative plural in -is). 'volvere fumum' means 'to roll smoke'. 'primum… tandem' together are 'first, at last'. 'ac' is a variant of 'atque', 'and'.

sentences.t: Vela cadunt, remis insurgimus;
sentences.l: The sails fall, we rise to the oars;
sentences.i: The sails come down, and we rise to the oars;
sentences.n: 'Vela cadunt' means 'the sails fall', they are lowered, since the oars are now needed. 'remis insurgimus' means 'we rise to the oars' (dative with 'insurgo').

sentences.t:
haud mora nautae
adnixi torquent spumas et caerula verrunt.
sentences.l:
no delay, the sailors
straining twist the foam and sweep the blue.
sentences.i: There is no delay; the sailors bend to it, whirl up the foam and rake the blue water.
sentences.n: 'haud mora' has 'est' understood, 'there is no delay'. 'nautae' is the subject of 'torquent' and 'verrunt'. 'adnixi' is the nominative plural of the perfect participle of the deponent 'adnitor', 'straining', with active sense. 'torquent spumas' means 'twist, whirl the foam', 'verrunt' is the present of 'verro', 'sweep'. 'caerula' is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'the blue (waters)'. The part ends in mid-voyage, with land in sight.
